source: My lord, the guard at the front gate of Elsinore appears to be nervous about something.
Is there a particular grievance you aim to air in light of this?
No, my lord. Just wondering if you knew the cause behind it.
Bernardo, no doubt. He keeps them in line with a swift hand and a strict command. They're all terrified of disappointing him.
Bernardo does a most excellent job of handling them. I trust all such matters of their odd behavior to him.
My lady, do you know why the guards would believe they were on 'thin ice' with Bernardo?
What's Bernardo got them doing now?
A few weeks ago, I'd heard a little rumor from Brit about a gambling circle of some kind in the evenings... run by Irma, no less.
And just a day later, I saw them running laps in the courtyard. Bernardo was there with a willow rod, smacking their heels if they were too slow. Even Irma was forced to run!
He really does take his work rather seriously.
So if they're starting trouble again, I've no doubt Bernardo should know about it!
I know the King keeps a private stash of poison in his chambers, and he intends to use it.
That's a rather insidious thing to assert, isn't it?
Only if you don't believe me.
You have access to his chambers. Can't you verify what I'm saying is true?
...The King would not want to hear of this, regardless of the veracity of your words.
But he's not always in his rooms. He often meanders.
I will investigate. I'll let you know if I find anything worthwhile.
That potato-headed clod would keep such a thing in such an obvious place, wouldn't he.
If harm might come to my lady as a result, then I cannot ignore this.
Do you know how to acquire a key to his rooms?
Wah hah hah! A key!
Girl, these walls are ancient. All doors are keyless if you have the right tools.
I will look into this so-called poison. And if I find anything, you will know.
My lady, your husband is keeping a private stash of poison in his chambers. I believe he intends to use it.
Faith, what are you saying, Ophelia?
Poison? For what purpose?
I... think the King may plan to use it to... eliminate Hamlet.
I'm sorry. I understand this must be difficult to hear. But if you can stop him, then your son will be safe.
I think he may have... planned to use it on Hamlet.
I'm sorry. I understand this must be difficult to hear.
I don't know whether to believe you, but I have a key to my husband's chambers.
At the very least, I can look around and see what I might find the next time he departs.
I... pray... I don't find anything. I truly do.
Your uncle keeps a private stash of poison in his chambers, and I believe he intends to use it.
That cannot come to pass.
Perhaps this is the proof I've been seeking.
Not even a locked door can stop me now.
I'll enter when he's gone and uncover the truth, one way or another.
I'll enter when he's gone and take his tools, one way or another.
Your Majesty, I know you keep a stash of poison in your innermost chambers, and that you plan to use it.
Poison! That's quite an accusation, girl.
And what leads you to believe something like that?
I know you used it to rid yourself of your brother. You can stop pretending you don't know what I'm talking about.
Ah. I see.
I wondered if something like that might happen. If you might betray my trust. My confidence.
Now I know that to be true.
I was the more deceived.
I came here not to assault you with this, but rather to let you know that... I understand.
I understand why you did it. Why you killed him.
That's all I think needs to be said.
I never saw myself as a man who would take his brother's life. Not once.
It was the sort of dark place I came to after years. Years of his hatred, his injustice.
It was all I could think of. It consumed me. I needed him gone.
Let-- Let us speak of that no more, Ophelia. Let it accumulate yesterdays upon its grave.
Father, I've learned Claudius keeps a stash of poison in his private chambers. Shouldn't we do something to rid him of it?
Oh, God above.
Certainly you must do nothing until such a claim has been verified, dearest.
For your own safety, and mine.
But certainly we have to find out whether or not the claim is true, don't we?
You always told me we had an obligation to be honest, to be brave.
If there's even a chance Claudius might use this poison, mustn't we stop him?
Drat. And to think, my own child parroting my wisdom back to me!
Very well. I shall have a look. But I promise nothing.
I have an old key from when King Hamlet occupied the room. I don't believe His Majesty has changed the locks.
I'll slip in when he goes for a stroll and see what I can find.
Don't take this the wrong way, but -- what if Hamlet and I began seeing each other again?
The 'wrong way', she says. Is there a right way to court Hamlet?
That was rhetorical, sister. You already know my feelings on this.
You'll put Father into an early grave that way.
Father's newly passed, and your head's already on ignoring the advice he spent so many months giving you.
So don't speak to me of this, but listen to your inner voice of reason. What does it tell you?
What do you know of Othello, the barkeep in town?
Ah. I've met the man himself, in fact, when I landed at his establishment.
After my ill-fated and too-soon return to Elsinore... I needed a drink.
A grand storyteller, they call him.
I've never met the man, but I know of him. A storyteller, they call him.
But... he's the only one like us. Who looks the way we do.
Of course, Ophelia. Do you think I didn't notice?
Aren't you the least bit curious about where he comes from? Why he's in Denmark?
Mother came to Denmark. It's not all that peculiar.
Oh, come on. Look around, Laertes. There is no one else like us. Mother was an oddity. We're oddities.
I know that just as well as you do.
I go walking through town at night, and everyone knows who I am. Everyone knows the little black lord, Polonius's son.
Every single day I struggle to keep my voice calm, my hands gentle.
I see how people flinch when I laugh too loudly, or glance at them across a darkened street.
And if I were to go and strike up a friendship with some no-name man who pours the ale... would they think me like him, then?
Because Ophelia, we are not like him. We are of noble blood.
And every moment we spend in the company of men like him, others will put us in the mold of some lower, baser image.
I don't believe that.
That you do not believe me is a blessing, for it means you truly don't know what strangers can be like.
Some day you'll understand.
Until then, be careful how you associate with Othello.
What do you know of Othello the barkeep?
It is what I try not to know that is of interest to you, I think.
He came to town only a short while ago, but has accumulated rather a lot of history in that span.
Though he tells a tall tale and has always shown me kindness, so I look away from it.
Sells the cheapest ale you can find in town!
And his patrons are some of the cheapest whores, too.
His lifestyle's catching up with him at last, of course. Men attacking at all hours of the day.
That sort of thing always catches up, in the end.
Guildenstern will not cease chattering about him, despite knowing almost nothing about him.
She fancies him a poet-warrior of sorts, or something like that. She's writing him a sonnet.
At this point, it's difficult to recall which things she's told me as fact versus girlish fantasy.
Cutest warrior-poet in all Denmark, if you ask me!
I'm writing him a sonnet!
How's it go?
Oh, Othello, who gives generous pours, and whom my soul adores...
That's it.
That's not a sonnet at all. Fourteen lines of ten syllables -- isn't that how it goes?
Stop putting labels on my art!
Mm. Let's see. Think he was a slave, then a warrior, then he escaped and was a pirate for a bit, and now he's here.
Mother's name was Adi... Told me his father's once, but I cannot recall it.
You know quite a lot, then.
Oh, yes. You see, I ask.
Isn't it strange how so many people never ask a true question of those around them?
It's always, 'how is your health?' Or 'isn't it lovely outside?' And never, 'what makes you truly happy?' or 'what was your mother like?'
Well, for everyone except you. You're quite the little inquisitor.
Always seem to be on the heels of your next interrogation.
Did you know Prince Hamlet and I were once in a relationship?
Ought I to be concerned you're telling me this?
I merely wanted to bring it to your attention.
You know, I am a man rather easily possessed of jealousy.
I-- I must admit it has been described to me as a fault of mine.
I have no qualms with your past, Ophelia. But that you raise this matter now...
Please don't trifle with me. I care for you too much for that nonsense, and we are far too grown for it besides.
Well, as you've shown little interest in me, I can only imagine the man still has your heart.
Will you go to him?
I thought I'd heard every rumor in the country, but I suppose I was short one.
Given your family resides at Elsinore, I imagine you had quite some time to make his acquaintance.
Tell me, was it a torch bursting to life? Or a slow-burning flame?
You are forward, aren't you.
I prefer to call it 'honest.' But please forgive me. Some find that honesty rather coarse.
What would you say if Hamlet and I were to rekindle our relationship?
Well, nothing nice, I suppose.
That's all you have to say on this?
Ophelia, I like to joke, and even this isn't funny to me.
For so many reasons, the least of which is my own history with Hamlet.
Must you be cruel?
Nothing, only to ask that you not say anything to Guildenstern about it.
She's-- well, she and Hamlet--
They weren't together long when we were at school, but she was left feeling sour over the whole ordeal.
Vita brevis, occasio praeceps.
'Life is short, opportunity fleeting?' What's that supposed to mean?
One ought to pursue whatever whim crosses one's mind. In this case, for you, Hamlet.
For if we all might be dead tomorrow, what good does it do to deny yourself a worldly pleasure today?
